"This poor widow hath cast more in, than all they which have cast into the treasury," he said; the others gave of their abundance, "but she of her want did cast in all that she had."
neighbors.difference: In Leviticus, the offerings make room for the poor, and the rabbis weigh the heart over the price. In the Gospel, Jesus himself names her gift, and many Christians read it as trusting God with everything.
neighbors.shared: the smallest gift can hold the most of you.

neighbors.heading: the mother of virtues
neighbors.text: Today the thanks offering came with forty loaves, too much to eat alone, so thanks became a party and a story. The Roman orator Cicero called gratitude not only the greatest of the virtues but the mother of all the rest. In his view, a grateful heart is where loyalty, friendship and kindness grow.
neighbors.difference: The todah thanks God for a rescue, out loud, with a meal shared among neighbors. Cicero praises gratitude as a human virtue owed to parents, friends and benefactors, a matter of character more than worship.
neighbors.shared: a grateful heart makes room at the table.

neighbors.heading: the great thank you
neighbors.text: Today a rescued person brought the thanks offering, and a midrash said thanks will outlast every other offering. Catholics name their central act of worship for thanks: Eucharist, from a Greek word for giving thanks. And a psalm they pray says: "Offer to God the sacrifice of praise: and pay thy vows to the most High."
neighbors.difference: The todah was an offering of bread and meat, kept today as a blessing said after danger. For Catholics, the Eucharist is thanks and also Christ's own sacrifice made present, received as his body and blood.
neighbors.shared: thank you may be the prayer that lasts longest.
neighbors.sources: Psalm 49:14 (Douay-Rheims; Psalm 50:14 in many Bibles) · Catechism of the Catholic Church 1328, 1360 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: a discipline of speech
neighbors.text: Today the rabbis read the skin affliction as harmful words finally showing. The Bhagavad Gita treats speech as a practice too. Krishna calls it austerity of speech: words that cause no distress, that are true, pleasant and helpful, along with steady study of sacred texts. What you say trains you as much as it reaches anyone else.
neighbors.difference: The rabbis tie harmful speech to a bodily sign and a time outside the camp. The Gita treats careful speech as tapas, an inner discipline that purifies the speaker on the path toward God.
neighbors.shared: words leave marks, so choose kind and true ones.

neighbors.heading: speaking of the absent
neighbors.text: Today the rabbis said harmful speech, even when true, finally shows on the skin. The Qur'an paints its own hard picture: "neither backbite one another. Would one of you love to eat the flesh of his dead brother? Ye abhor that." Muslims call it ghibah, and the Prophet explained it: mentioning your brother in a way he'd hate, even if it's true.
neighbors.difference: The rabbis read tzara'at as a visible sign for harmful speech, examined by a priest. The Qur'an names backbiting directly, with an image, and Muslims seek forgiveness from God and, where they can, from the person.
neighbors.shared: speak about the absent as if they were in the room.

neighbors.heading: he touched him
neighbors.text: Today the priest walked out of the camp to the person who couldn't come in. The Gospels tell of a man with leprosy who knelt before Jesus: "And Jesus, moved with compassion, put forth his hand, and touched him." Christians have followed that hand to sickbeds ever since, remembering his words: "I was sick, and ye visited me."
neighbors.difference: In Leviticus the priest goes out to look and to restore the person to the camp. Christians believe Jesus healed with that touch, and they serve the sick as if serving Christ himself.
neighbors.shared: when someone can't come in, go out to them.

neighbors.heading: care at Tarn Taran
neighbors.text: Today the priest went outside the camp to the person who had to live there. Sikh tradition remembers Guru Arjan founding the town of Tarn Taran and caring there for people with leprosy, whom others shunned. And Guru Har Krishan, still a child, is remembered tending the sick during an epidemic in Delhi.
neighbors.difference: The Torah's priest goes out to examine and bring the person back into the camp. The Gurus' care is remembered as seva, service to the sick that sees the One in everyone.
neighbors.shared: no one should be left outside alone.
neighbors.sources: Sikh tradition on Guru Arjan at Tarn Taran and Guru Har Krishan in Delhi (paraphrase)

items.lessonTitle: Acharei Mot: ask the person first (Mishnah Yoma 8:9)

neighbors.heading: leave thy gift
neighbors.text: Today the Mishnah said Yom Kippur can't mend a wrong between people until you go to them first. Jesus teaches the same order: "If therefore thou offer thy gift at the altar, and there thou remember that thy brother hath any thing against thee; Leave there thy offering before the altar, and go first to be reconciled to thy brother."
neighbors.difference: Jews make things right with people, then turn to God on Yom Kippur. Catholics also have confession, where they believe God forgives through the priest, yet a wrong done to a person still calls for repair.
neighbors.shared: before you face heaven, face the person you hurt.

neighbors.heading: two kinds of fools
neighbors.text: Today the Mishnah said you must go to the person you wronged and ask their forgiveness. A Buddhist scripture tells of two monks who quarreled. One went too far, admitted it and asked pardon; the other wouldn't accept. The Buddha said there are two kinds of fools: one who won't see his wrong, and one who won't forgive the person confessing.
neighbors.difference: In Jewish teaching, Yom Kippur sets a season for asking, and God forgives what lies between people and God. Buddhists confess and forgive without turning to God; it clears the mind and mends the community.
neighbors.shared: say sorry plainly, and let sorry be received.

neighbors.heading: love for your brother
neighbors.text: Today Leviticus said love your neighbor as yourself, and Rabbi Akiva called it a great principle. The Prophet Muhammad said something close, in a saying Muslims learn young: none of you truly believes until he loves for his brother what he loves for himself. Some scholars read brother there as every human being.
neighbors.difference: Leviticus is a command of the Torah, sealed with I am the LORD. The Muslim teaching is a hadith, a saying of the Prophet, and it ties love of others to the completeness of a person's faith.
neighbors.shared: want for others the good you want for yourself.

neighbors.heading: one word for a lifetime
neighbors.text: Today Hillel summed up the Torah: what is hateful to you, don't do to your neighbor. In China, a student once asked Confucius for one word to live by. The answer: "Is not RECIPROCITY such a word? What you do not want done to yourself, do not do to others."
neighbors.difference: Leviticus seals its command with I am the LORD: love of neighbor is asked by God. Confucius roots reciprocity in human relationships and good character rather than in a divine command.
neighbors.shared: treat others the way you hope to be treated.

neighbors.heading: a room in the True One's house
neighbors.text: Today the Torah said the land is God's, and you are strangers and settlers with God. Sikh scripture speaks the same way: this world is the room of the True One, and the True One lives in it. And Japji Sahib closes by calling the earth the great mother of all. You live here fully, and you're still a guest.
neighbors.difference: The Torah turns the idea into law: land returns to its families in the jubilee year. Sikh scripture turns it inward: the world is God's dwelling, and seeing that loosens pride in what you hold.
neighbors.shared: you live here as a guest, so treat the house gently.
neighbors.sources: Guru Granth Sahib, Asa di Var, Ang 463 (paraphrase) · Japji Sahib, closing salok, Ang 8 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: enjoy it by letting go
neighbors.text: Today the Torah said the land can't be sold forever: it's God's, and you are guests. The Isha Upanishad opens on the same note. All this, whatever moves in the world, is dwelt in by the Lord. So enjoy it by letting go, the verse says, and don't covet anyone's wealth. You can use the world without owning it.
neighbors.difference: In Leviticus the land is God's gift to a people, returned to its families every fiftieth year. The Upanishad speaks to each person's inner life: seeing the Lord in all things loosens the grip of mine.
neighbors.shared: what you hold is borrowed, and that's a gentle thing.

neighbors.heading: teacher as father
neighbors.text: Today the Talmud said whoever teaches someone's child is counted as their parent. The Buddha set up the same bond among monks. The monastic rules say a teacher should look on a student as a son, and the student on the teacher as a father, each caring for the other in study, in sickness and in daily needs.
neighbors.difference: The Talmud's teacher passes on Torah inside a family of generations. The Buddhist bond is between monastics who left home: a new family gathered around the Dharma, aimed at freedom from suffering.
neighbors.shared: whoever teaches you with love becomes family.

neighbors.heading: not many fathers
neighbors.text: Today Moses was counted as a father to Aaron's sons because he taught them. Paul wrote to the church he founded in Corinth in nearly the same way: "For though ye have ten thousand instructers in Christ, yet have ye not many fathers: for in Christ Jesus I have begotten you through the gospel."
neighbors.difference: The Talmud honors teachers of Torah as parents within the Jewish people. Paul calls himself a father because he first brought the Corinthians to faith in Christ, a new birth Christians believe the gospel brings.
neighbors.shared: the one who teaches you is part of your family tree.

neighbors.heading: the repair in an apology
neighbors.text: Today the Torah said a wrong is confessed in words, then repaid with a fifth added. Researchers who studied apologies found the same two steps matter most. The parts people valued highest were saying plainly that it was my fault, and offering to fix what was broken. Simply asking for forgiveness counted least.
neighbors.difference: In Numbers, a wrong to a neighbor is also a wrong against God, so confession turns toward heaven too. The research looks only at people: what makes an apology land with the one you hurt.
neighbors.shared: say what you did, then make it right.
neighbors.sources: Roy Lewicki, Beth Polin and Robert Lount, "An Exploration of the Structure of Effective Apologies," Negotiation and Conflict Management Research, 2016 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: fourfold
neighbors.text: Today the Torah said a wrong is confessed aloud and repaid with a fifth added. Catholics confess their sins aloud to a priest in the sacrament of penance, and the Church teaches that what was taken must be given back. In the Gospel, the tax collector Zacheus goes further still: "if I have wronged any man of any thing, I restore him fourfold."
neighbors.difference: In Numbers, confession is spoken and repayment goes straight to the person wronged. Catholics confess to a priest, believing God forgives through him in Christ's name, and restitution is part of making amends afterward.
neighbors.shared: sorry means more when your hands make it right.
neighbors.sources: Luke 19:8 (Douay-Rheims) · Catechism of the Catholic Church 1459, 2412 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: no effort is lost
neighbors.text: Today people who missed Passover asked for a chance, and got a second date. In the Bhagavad Gita, Arjuna asks a worried question: what happens to someone who sets out on the path and falls short? Krishna answers that no one who does good comes to grief. The seeker picks up where they left off and keeps going.
neighbors.difference: Pesach Sheni gives a second date, one month later, in this same life. In the Gita, the next chance may come in a future birth, where the seeker's earlier effort carries forward.
neighbors.shared: falling short isn't the end of the road.

neighbors.heading: other days
neighbors.text: Today the Torah gave a second Passover to those who were impure or far away on a journey. The Qur'an makes room the same way in the fast of Ramadan: "and (for) him who is sick among you, or on a journey, (the same) number of other days." Missed for a reason, kept later.
neighbors.difference: Pesach Sheni is one set date, a month later, for those kept back. The Qur'an lets the one who missed choose other days, and those who can't fast at all may feed a needy person instead.
neighbors.shared: if life gets in the way, the door opens again.

items.lessonTitle: Korach: Moses falls on his face (Numbers 16:4)

neighbors.heading: slow to speak
neighbors.text: Today Moses heard the crowd's attack and fell on his face before saying a word. The letter of James gives Christians that same order: "let every man be swift to hear, slow to speak, slow to wrath." And when Jesus was accused before the high priest, the Gospel says simply: "But Jesus held his peace."
neighbors.difference: Moses' fall is read as distress or prayer before facing rebels. Christians see in Jesus' silence before his accusers a willing path to the cross, which they believe saves the world.
neighbors.shared: a pause before answering can keep a fight from catching fire.

neighbors.heading: sweetness and humility
neighbors.text: Today Moses fell to the ground before answering an angry crowd. Guru Nanak says sweetness and humility are the essence of every good quality. And Sheikh Farid, whose verses sit in the Sikh scripture, asks for more: answer evil with good, and don't let anger fill your mind. The humble answer is often the strongest one.
neighbors.difference: Moses falls on his face before God and the people, then confronts the rebels. Sikh teaching asks for humility as a whole way of life, joined with the courage to stand against injustice.
neighbors.shared: a humble pause can be stronger than a sharp reply.
neighbors.sources: Guru Granth Sahib, Asa di Var, Ang 470, Guru Nanak (paraphrase) · Salok Sheikh Farid, Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1381–1382 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: blessed are the peacemakers
neighbors.text: Today all Israel wept for Aaron, the man who ran after peace between quarreling friends. Jesus gave peacemakers a blessing of their own: "Blessed are the peacemakers: for they shall be called the children of God." And at Mass, just before Communion, Catholics turn to the people beside them and offer a sign of peace.
neighbors.difference: Aaron, a priest, is honored for patiently reconciling people, sometimes with a gentle nudge. Catholics see Christ himself as the source of peace, and share his peace at Mass before receiving Communion.
neighbors.shared: running after peace is a kind of holiness.
neighbors.sources: Matthew 5:9 (Douay-Rheims) · the sign of peace at Mass (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: a mender of quarrels
neighbors.text: Today Aaron was mourned as one who loved peace and pursued it. Buddhist scripture praises the same gift, describing one who brings together those who are divided and speaks words that make for peace. And the Dhammapada says: "hatred does not cease by hatred at any time: hatred ceases by love, this is an old rule."
neighbors.difference: Aaron pursued peace as a priest serving God and his people. In Buddhist teaching, peacemaking speech is part of right speech on the path to freedom from suffering, and doesn't rest on God.
neighbors.shared: a life spent mending quarrels is a life well spent.
neighbors.sources: Digha Nikaya 1, Brahmajala Sutta (paraphrase) · Dhammapada 5 (Max Müller 1881)

neighbors.heading: a share for the women
neighbors.text: Today five sisters asked for their father's land, and God said they speak right. The Qur'an also writes women into inheritance: "Unto the men (of a family) belongeth a share of that which parents and near kindred leave, and unto the women a share of that which parents and near kindred leave."
neighbors.difference: In Numbers, daughters inherit when there are no sons, after five sisters asked. The Qur'an sets fixed shares for daughters alongside sons, often half a son's share, which Muslim scholars tie to a son's duty to provide.
neighbors.shared: daughters belong in a family's story, and in its inheritance.

neighbors.heading: wrong in itself
neighbors.text: Today five sisters asked, in public, why the law should erase them, and the law changed. Much later, the philosopher John Stuart Mill made a case in reason's terms. He argued that keeping one sex legally under the other is wrong in itself, and one of the chief things holding human progress back.
neighbors.difference: The sisters bring their case to Moses, and God answers, making it law. Mill argues from reason and human progress alone, appealing to no revelation.
neighbors.shared: asking for what's fair can open the door for everyone after you.
neighbors.sources: John Stuart Mill, The Subjection of Women (1869), chapter 1 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: nitnem, the daily rhythm
neighbors.text: Today two lambs a day, morning and evening, became the backbone of Jewish prayer. Sikhs keep a daily rhythm too, called nitnem. In the early morning, Japji Sahib and other prayers; at sunset, Rehras Sahib; at bedtime, Kirtan Sohila. The day is held between words of praise, the way two lambs once held the day in the sanctuary.
neighbors.difference: Jewish prayer times grew from the Temple's offerings and the patriarchs. Sikh daily prayers are the Gurus' own compositions, recited or sung, meant to keep God's Name in mind all day long.
neighbors.shared: begin and end the day on the same thread of prayer.

neighbors.heading: the joints of the day
neighbors.text: Today a lamb at morning and a lamb at evening set the rhythm of Jewish prayer. Hindu tradition has sandhya, prayer at the joints of the day: dawn and dusk, and sometimes noon. At its heart is the Gayatri mantra, a prayer that the light of the divine sun may brighten the mind, said as the sun rises and as it sets.
neighbors.difference: The tamid was a Temple offering that became prayer when the Temple fell. Sandhya is offered at home or by water, facing the sun, a practice tied especially to those who have received the sacred thread.
neighbors.shared: dawn and dusk are good places to stop and pray.
neighbors.sources: Rig Veda 3.62.10, the Gayatri mantra (paraphrase) · the sandhya-vandana tradition (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: last words
neighbors.text: Today Deuteronomy began: one long farewell, Moses speaking to the people he loves. The Buddha's last days are told too, in the Great Discourse on his passing. His final words to the monks gathered around him: "Decay is inherent in all component things! Work out your salvation with diligence!"
neighbors.difference: Moses' farewell retells a people's story and law before they cross into the land. The Buddha's last words point each listener inward: everything made will pass, so keep practicing toward freedom.
neighbors.shared: the last words of someone who loves you are worth keeping.
neighbors.sources: Digha Nikaya 16, Maha-parinibbana Sutta, chapter 6 (Rhys Davids)

neighbors.heading: a farewell at the table
neighbors.text: Today Deuteronomy opened: the whole book is Moses' last long talk with the people he loves. The Gospel of John slows down for a farewell too. At his last supper, Jesus talks with his friends for chapters, and says: "A new commandment I give unto you, That ye love one another; as I have loved you."
neighbors.difference: Moses speaks knowing he won't cross the river with them. Christians read Jesus' farewell knowing he goes to the cross, and believe he rose and is with them still.
neighbors.shared: what's said last, with love, gets carried longest.

neighbors.heading: what is up to us
neighbors.text: Today Moses pleaded to enter the land and heard: let it suffice thee. Then he climbed the mountain and looked anyway. The Stoic teacher Epictetus begins his handbook in the same place: "Of things some are in our power, and others are not." Long for what isn't yours to decide, and you suffer; give your strength to what is.
neighbors.difference: Moses' no comes from God, inside a living conversation, and comfort follows. Epictetus starts from nature and reason: some things simply aren't yours to choose.
neighbors.shared: a no can still leave you a mountain to stand on.

neighbors.heading: not my will
neighbors.text: Today Moses begged to cross into the land and heard: let it suffice thee. Catholics remember another plea, in a garden the night before the cross: "Father, if thou wilt, remove this chalice from me: but yet not my will, but thine be done." They pray it in the rosary as the agony in the garden.
neighbors.difference: Moses' plea is refused, and he dies within sight of the land. Catholics believe Jesus' yes in the garden led through his death to the resurrection, and they join their own hard yeses to his.
neighbors.shared: even a hard no can be met with trust.

neighbors.heading: who is the doer?
neighbors.text: Today Moses warned against saying: my power and the might of my hand got me this. The Bhagavad Gita names the same slip. All actions are done by the forces of nature, Krishna says, but a mind confused by ego thinks, I am the doer. The wise act fully and still don't claim it all for themselves.
neighbors.difference: Deuteronomy says God gives the power to get wealth, so you remember and bless. The Gita says action flows through nature's qualities, and seeing that loosens the ego, freeing a person to act as an offering.
neighbors.shared: your hands are real, and they had a lot of help.

neighbors.heading: on account of knowledge
neighbors.text: Today Moses warned against saying: my power and the might of my hand got me this. The Qur'an tells of Qarun, rich beyond measure, whose people told him not to exult. He answered: "I have been given it only on account of knowledge I possess." His story ends with the earth swallowing him and his house.
neighbors.difference: Deuteronomy warns a whole people, full and settled, not to forget. The Qur'an tells it through one proud man, whom Muslim commentators often link with Korach, and urges spending wealth in God's way.
neighbors.shared: what you have came with help, so hold it gratefully.

neighbors.heading: an open heart
neighbors.text: Today the Torah said: don't harden your heart or shut your hand; surely open it. A letter of John asks the same thing as a question: "But whoso hath this world's good, and seeth his brother have need, and shutteth up his bowels of compassion from him, how dwelleth the love of God in him?" Heart and hand open together.
neighbors.difference: Tzedakah means justice: giving is part of what's owed in a fair society. Christians usually speak of charity, from the Latin for love, and see giving to the needy as love shown to Christ himself.
neighbors.shared: an open heart shows up as an open hand.

neighbors.heading: something from your hand
neighbors.text: Today the Torah said: surely open thy hand to someone in need. Guru Nanak puts giving in the hand too: the one who works for what he eats and gives some of it from his own hand, he says, recognizes the path. Sikhs call it vand chhakna, sharing what you earn, and langar feeds anyone who walks in.
neighbors.difference: Tzedakah is a duty of justice, with Maimonides' levels for how to give. Sikh sharing grows out of honest work and remembering God's Name, and langar seats everyone on the floor together, as equals.
neighbors.shared: what your hands earn, your hands can share.
neighbors.sources: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1245, Guru Nanak (paraphrase) · Sikh Rehat Maryada, on langar (paraphrase)

items.lessonTitle: Shoftim: is the tree a man? (Deuteronomy 20:19)

neighbors.heading: that nothing be lost
neighbors.text: Today the rabbis built a whole law from a fruit tree: bal tashchit, don't destroy needlessly. After Jesus fed the five thousand, the Gospel adds a small instruction: "Gather up the fragments that remain, lest they be lost." The Church teaches that creation is a gift held in trust, to be cared for, not wasted.
neighbors.difference: Bal tashchit is a law with details: trees, dishes, food, even costlier bread. Catholics speak of stewardship of creation, and see the gathered fragments as signs of the abundance Christ gives.
neighbors.shared: the world is too precious to throw away.
neighbors.sources: John 6:12 (Douay-Rheims) · Catechism of the Catholic Church 2415 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: the robe becomes a wall
neighbors.text: Today the rabbis turned a fruit tree in wartime into a law against needless waste. Buddhist monks tell a story about robes. A king asked Ananda what the monks did with so many. Old robes become bedcovers, Ananda said; old bedcovers become floor coverings, then foot towels, and at last, shredded and mixed with clay, plaster for the walls.
neighbors.difference: Bal tashchit grows from God's command and honors what God made. The monks' thrift comes from the Buddha's path of simplicity and care for what lay donors give, with no command from God behind it.
neighbors.shared: even the last scrap can still be useful.

neighbors.heading: due on harvest day
neighbors.text: Today the farmer carried the first fruits in a basket and told his people's story. The Qur'an ties harvest and giving together too. Speaking of gardens, olives and pomegranates, it says: "Eat ye of the fruit thereof when it fruiteth, and pay the due thereof upon the harvest day." Muslims give zakat on crops when they're gathered.
neighbors.difference: Bikkurim was the first of the fruit, brought to the Temple with a spoken story. Zakat on crops is a set share for the poor and others in need, one of the pillars of Islam rather than a sanctuary offering.
neighbors.shared: the harvest is a gift, and gifts are for sharing.

neighbors.heading: counting blessings
neighbors.text: Today the farmer didn't say look what I grew; he told the story of everything that brought him there. Psychologists tested a small version. In one study, people wrote down a few things they were grateful for each week. After ten weeks, they felt better about their lives and more hopeful about the week ahead than people who listed hassles.
neighbors.difference: The farmer's thanks goes to God, said aloud at the sanctuary with priest and neighbors. The study measures what gratitude does for the person writing, without asking whom it's addressed to.
neighbors.shared: noticing where the good came from changes how the day feels.
neighbors.sources: Robert Emmons and Michael McCullough, "Counting Blessings Versus Burdens," Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 2003 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: why search the forest?
neighbors.text: Today Moses said the word isn't in heaven or across the sea: it's very near, in your mouth and in your heart. Sikhs sing something close. Guru Tegh Bahadur asks why anyone goes searching in the forest. The One lives in everything and stays with you, he says, like fragrance inside a flower, like a reflection in a mirror.
neighbors.difference: Moses means the Torah's teaching is near enough to say, understand and do. Guru Tegh Bahadur means God's own presence is already within, found by remembering the Name with the Guru's help.
neighbors.shared: what matters most isn't a long journey away.
neighbors.sources: Guru Tegh Bahadur, Raag Dhanasari, Guru Granth Sahib Ang 684 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: closer than the mountaintop
neighbors.text: Today Moses took apart the excuse of distance: the word is very near, in your mouth and in your heart. Hindus hear an echo in the Bhagavad Gita. Near its end, Krishna tells Arjuna that the Lord dwells in the heart of every being. No mountain to climb, no sea to cross: the search can begin right where you're sitting.
neighbors.difference: For Moses, what's near is the Torah given at Sinai, a teaching to live. In the Gita, what's near is the Lord himself, seated in every heart, met through devotion and self-knowledge.
neighbors.shared: the first step is closer than you think.

neighbors.heading: one rain, many plants
neighbors.text: Today Moses said teaching falls like rain, and the Sifrei added: the same rain helps the vine, the olive and the fig each grow its own way. Buddhists tell almost the same picture. In the Lotus Sutra, the Buddha compares his teaching to one great cloud raining on every plant alike, grasses, shrubs and tall trees. Each drinks what it can hold, and grows.
neighbors.difference: In the Torah, the rain is God's teaching through Moses to a people. In the Lotus Sutra, it's the Dharma, the Buddha's teaching for waking up, offered to every being; no creator sends it.
neighbors.shared: good teaching lands gently, and lets each person grow as themselves.
neighbors.sources: Lotus Sutra, chapter 5, the parable of the medicinal herbs (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: first the blade
neighbors.text: Today Moses said teaching comes like dew: slowly, overnight, and nobody sees it arrive. Jesus told a parable with the same patience. A man scatters seed, sleeps and rises, and the seed grows, "he knoweth not how." The earth does its quiet work: "first the blade, then the ear, after that the full corn in the ear."
neighbors.difference: Jesus says this is what the kingdom of God is like, a kingdom Christians see beginning in him. For Jews, the gentle rain is the Torah, given at Sinai and learned a little at a time.
neighbors.shared: what grows slowly is still growing.

neighbors.heading: a question at both ends
neighbors.text: Today the Talmud said Abraham prayed in the morning, Isaac in the field at evening, Jacob as night fell. People with no fixed religion keep set pauses too. Benjamin Franklin planned his days around two questions. At dawn: "What good shall I do this day?" At night: "What good have I done to-day?"
neighbors.difference: Jewish prayer three times a day is spoken to God, in set words, often with a community. Franklin's questions were his own, asked of himself; he used them to build good habits, not to pray.
neighbors.shared: a day goes better with a few set pauses.
neighbors.sources: Benjamin Franklin, Autobiography, the scheme of his day

neighbors.heading: morning, noon and evening
neighbors.text: Today the Talmud tied three daily prayers to Abraham, Isaac and Jacob. Catholics keep set hours too. A psalm sings: "Evening and morning, and at noon I will speak and declare: and he shall hear my voice." The Angelus is traditionally prayed morning, noon and evening, and the Liturgy of the Hours marks prayer through the whole day.
neighbors.difference: The Angelus remembers the angel's message to Mary and God becoming flesh in Jesus. The Jewish prayers at these hours are the Amidah, rooted in the patriarchs and the Temple's daily offerings.
neighbors.shared: the clock itself can call you back to prayer.
neighbors.sources: Psalm 54:18 (Douay-Rheims; Psalm 55:17 in many Bibles) · the Angelus (description)

items.lessonTitle: The soul you gave me is pure

neighbors.heading: what fire cannot burn
neighbors.text: Today's prayer began: my God, the soul you placed in me is pure. Hindus speak of a self beneath everything a day can throw at it. In the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna tells Arjuna that weapons cannot cut the true self, fire cannot burn it, water cannot wet it, wind cannot dry it. Moods and mistakes come and go; the atman stays untouched.
neighbors.difference: The Jewish prayer thanks God, who created the soul, breathed it in, and returns it each morning. In the Gita, the atman was never born and never dies; some Hindu schools teach it is one with Brahman itself.
neighbors.shared: underneath a hard day, something in you stays clean.

neighbors.heading: life after a little sleep
neighbors.text: Today's prayer thanked God for giving the soul back each morning. Muslims wake with words like it. Prophet Muhammad taught them to say: praise be to God, who gave us life after He made us die, and to Him is the rising. The Qur'an says God takes souls at death, and in sleep too, and sends back those whose time hasn't come.
neighbors.difference: Elohai Neshamah calls the soul pure and hopes for its return in the time to come. The Muslim waking words come from the Prophet's practice, and point ahead to the Day of Rising.
neighbors.shared: every morning is a small gift handed back.
neighbors.sources: Sahih al-Bukhari, Book of Invocations, words on waking (paraphrase) · Qur'an 39:42 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: I was sick, and ye visited me
neighbors.text: Today's list had no limits: taking in guests, visiting the sick, walking with the dead. Jesus told of a day when the king says, "I was a stranger, and ye took me in: Naked, and ye clothed me: I was sick, and ye visited me." Surprised, people ask when. The answer: whatever you did for the least of these, you did for me.
neighbors.difference: In Matthew, Jesus is the king, and caring for the least is caring for him. In the Jewish list, these are mitzvot done by walking in God's ways, with fruit in this life and the principal kept for the world to come.
neighbors.shared: showing up for someone counts more than we know.

neighbors.heading: seva, with your own hands
neighbors.text: Today's list said kindness done with your own body has no limit. Sikhs call that seva, selfless service. Guru Nanak taught that serving in this world earns a place of honor in God's court. In a gurdwara, seva looks like chopping onions, washing dishes, sweeping floors and cooking in the langar, the free kitchen where anyone sits and eats, side by side.
neighbors.difference: The Jewish list names particular deeds, like helping a bride marry or escorting the dead, and sets Torah study equal to them all. For Sikhs, seva goes hand in hand with simran, remembering God's Name, done without ego.
neighbors.shared: the hands can pray too.
neighbors.sources: Guru Nanak, Sri Raag, Guru Granth Sahib Ang 26 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: the thanksgiving that lasts
neighbors.text: Today a midrash said every offering will one day cease except thanks. Catholics give their central prayer a name about thanks: the Eucharist. The Catechism calls it an action of thanksgiving to God, and a sacrifice of thanksgiving to the Father. At every Mass, the priest invites the people to lift up their hearts and give thanks.
neighbors.difference: For Catholics, the Eucharist makes present Christ's own sacrifice, the thanks he gave at the Last Supper. For Jews, the Temple's thanksgiving offering lives on in words: a psalm, said with joy.
neighbors.shared: of everything we offer, thanks is the part that lasts.

neighbors.heading: living happily
neighbors.text: Today's psalm said serve with gladness, with real joy. Buddhists count joy as part of the path, not only a reward at the end. Joy, piti, is one of the seven factors of awakening. And a chapter of the Dhammapada called Happiness begins: let us live happily, free of hatred among those who hate. Gladness here is a skill you practice.
neighbors.difference: The psalm's joy is offered to God, who is served with gladness. For Buddhists, joy grows from a calm, clear mind and generous living, a step toward awakening, with no creator to thank.
neighbors.shared: a glad heart is part of the work, not a break from it.
neighbors.sources: Dhammapada 197 (paraphrase) · the seven factors of awakening, Samyutta Nikaya 46 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: say: He is One
neighbors.text: Today the Shema drew out one word long enough to mean it: echad, one. Muslims say that oneness in their own words. The Qur'an's short chapter 112 begins: "Say: He is Allah, the One!" Muslims call God's oneness tawhid, and Prophet Muhammad said this little chapter equals a third of the Qur'an.
neighbors.difference: The Shema is said to Israel, hand over the eyes, from the Torah. Muslims declare God's oneness in the Qur'an's Arabic, and their testimony of faith joins it to Muhammad as God's messenger.
neighbors.shared: one word, said slowly, can gather a whole life.
neighbors.sources: Qur'an 112:1 (Pickthall) · Sahih al-Bukhari, on Surah al-Ikhlas (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: what you agree to attend to
neighbors.text: Today Rabbi Judah covered his eyes for one line, to attend to one thing. The psychologist William James saw how much rides on that. "My experience is what I agree to attend to," he wrote. "Only those items which I notice shape my mind." Close your eyes, gather your attention, and you choose, a little, who you become.
neighbors.difference: The Shema gathers attention to declare God's oneness, said as a witness. James was describing how a mind works; you can follow him with no belief in God at all.
neighbors.shared: where you put your attention, your life follows.
neighbors.sources: William James, The Principles of Psychology (1890), chapter 11, "Attention"

neighbors.heading: remember, remember
neighbors.text: Today the fringes said: look, remember, do. Sikhs build a life around remembering too. They call it simran. Guru Arjan's Sukhmani Sahib begins with it: remember, remember, remember God, and find peace. Sikhs keep set prayers morning and evening, and some repeat Waheguru through the day, so remembering isn't left to chance.
neighbors.difference: Tzitzit remind the wearer of the commandments, and to do them, with the Exodus recalled night and morning. Simran keeps God's Name itself on the tongue and in the heart, a way to live in God's presence.
neighbors.shared: we all need help remembering what matters.
neighbors.sources: Guru Arjan, Sukhmani Sahib, Guru Granth Sahib Ang 262 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: beads in the hand
neighbors.text: Today the fringes gave the eyes something to look at, so the heart would remember. Many Hindus keep a reminder in the hand: a japa mala, a string of beads, moving one bead for each repetition of God's name. In the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna tells Arjuna to remember him at all times, even in the middle of his duty.
neighbors.difference: The fringes point to the commandments and to the Exodus, a people's story. The mala counts the name of a chosen form of God, and in the Gita, remembering Krishna is a path of devotion.
neighbors.shared: a small thing you can touch can call you home.

neighbors.heading: whoever would tend me
neighbors.text: Today's blessing said power is the power to catch: support the falling, heal the sick. Buddhists tell of the Buddha finding a monk lying sick and untended, in his own filth. The Buddha and Ananda washed him and laid him on a bed. Then the Buddha told the monks: whoever would care for me should care for the sick.
neighbors.difference: In the Amidah, catching the falling is first God's might, which people copy by walking in God's ways. In the Buddhist story, a teacher sets the example, and caring for the sick is the practice itself.
neighbors.shared: the strongest hands are the ones that catch someone.

neighbors.heading: liberty to the bruised
neighbors.text: Today's blessing listed what God's might is for: healing the sick, freeing the bound. In Luke, Jesus stands up in the synagogue at Nazareth and reads from Isaiah: "to preach deliverance to the captives, and recovering of sight to the blind, to set at liberty them that are bruised." Then the gospel follows him healing and lifting people up.
neighbors.difference: Luke has Jesus say, "This day is this scripture fulfilled in your ears," and Christians see these deeds in him. Jews praise God for them in every weekday Amidah, and take them up as a job list.
neighbors.shared: real power bends down to lift someone.

neighbors.heading: a daily court
neighbors.text: Today's blessing made forgiveness daily maintenance, easier when it doesn't build up. The Roman philosopher Seneca kept a habit like it. Each night, once the lamp was out, he went over his whole day, word by word, hiding nothing from himself. Then he'd tell himself: see that you don't do that again; this time, I forgive you.
neighbors.difference: In the Amidah, people ask God to forgive, tapping the chest and speaking as we. Seneca was his own judge, reviewing the day by reason so he could do better; no prayer was needed.
neighbors.shared: a little honesty every night keeps the heart light.

neighbors.heading: a hand on the heart
neighbors.text: Today, at "we have sinned," many tapped their chest. Catholics strike the breast too. At Mass, confessing to God and to one another, they say mea culpa, through my fault, three times. Jesus told of a tax collector who stood far off, struck his breast, and said: "O God, be merciful to me a sinner."
neighbors.difference: Catholics also bring sins to a priest in the sacrament of Penance, where forgiveness is given in Christ's name. In the Amidah, Jews ask God directly for forgiveness every weekday, in the plural.
neighbors.shared: an honest knock on the heart opens the door to mercy.

neighbors.heading: speech that doesn't wound
neighbors.text: Today's closing prayer asked: guard my tongue from evil. Hindus count gentle speech as a discipline. In the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna describes the austerity of speech: words that cause no distress, words that are true, kind and helpful, and the steady habit of sacred study. Speech, in this view, is something you train, like the body.
neighbors.difference: Elohai Netzor asks God to guard the tongue, and to let the soul be silent toward those who curse. In the Gita, gentle speech is tapas, a discipline a person practices, offered without craving its fruit.
neighbors.shared: every kind word is a small act of care.

neighbors.heading: speak good, or keep silent
neighbors.text: Today's prayer asked God to guard the tongue, and the lips from deceit. Muslims carry a saying of Prophet Muhammad for the same moment: whoever believes in God and the Last Day, let them speak good or stay silent. The Qur'an names backbiting too, and pictures it as ugly as eating a dead brother's flesh.
neighbors.difference: Elohai Netzor began as one rabbi's private prayer, asking God's help. The Muslim saying is the Prophet's teaching, part of what believers say faith itself looks like.
neighbors.shared: silence can be a kindness too.
neighbors.sources: Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim, "speak good or keep silent" (paraphrase) · Qur'an 49:12 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: for all in authority
neighbors.text: Today the synagogue prayed for the sick, the congregation and the country, even, Jeremiah said, for the city of exile. Christians were asked for the same. Paul wrote that "supplications, prayers, intercessions, and giving of thanks, be made for all men; For kings, and for all that are in authority; that we may lead a quiet and peaceable life."
neighbors.difference: Paul goes on to name one mediator between God and people, Christ Jesus, and Christians pray in his name. The Mi Sheberach asks the One who blessed Abraham, Isaac and Jacob to bless each person by name.
neighbors.shared: praying for others makes a stranger's good your own.

neighbors.heading: the good of all
neighbors.text: Today's prayers moved outward, from one sick friend to the whole country. Sikhs end their communal prayer, the Ardas, by moving outward too. After remembering the Gurus and asking for the day's needs, it closes with a wish for everyone: in your will, may all be well. Sikhs call it sarbat da bhala, the good of all.
neighbors.difference: The Mi Sheberach names people one by one: the sick, a new baby, the country. The Ardas reaches for all humanity at once, with chardi kala, rising spirits, through God's Name.
neighbors.shared: a prayer can hold the whole world, one name at a time.

neighbors.heading: a holy and wholesome thought
neighbors.text: Today mourners stood for Kaddish, and the room answered. Catholics pray for their dead too. Their Bible praises Judas Maccabeus for it: "It is therefore a holy and wholesome thought to pray for the dead." Catholics have Masses offered for those who've died, and remember them on anniversaries and every November, on All Souls' Day.
neighbors.difference: Catholics pray that the dead be purified and brought into God's presence. The Kaddish never mentions death: the mourner praises God's name, and Jewish tradition holds that this praise helps the soul.
neighbors.shared: love keeps speaking after a goodbye.
neighbors.sources: 2 Maccabees 12:46 (Douay-Rheims) · Catechism of the Catholic Church 1032 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: sharing merit with the dead
neighbors.text: Today a mourner came out of the house to say Kaddish, and the community answered. Buddhists gather for their dead too. In an old Buddhist text, relatives give food and gifts to monks in a dead person's name, then share the goodness of that gift with them. The custom lives on at funerals and remembrance days.
neighbors.difference: The Kaddish is praise of God, said by a mourner with a minyan. Buddhists address no creator; they make merit through generosity and dedicate it to the one who died, wishing them well wherever they are.
neighbors.shared: grief is lighter when the community answers.

items.lessonTitle: A good thing to give thanks (Psalm 92:2)

neighbors.heading: give thanks, and receive more
neighbors.text: Today's Sabbath psalm said it is a good thing to give thanks, morning and night. Every Muslim prayer includes the Fatiha, which begins: al-hamdu lillah, praise be to God. And the Qur'an carries a promise: "If ye give thanks, I will give you more." Thanks, shukr, is said after a meal, good news, even a hard day.
neighbors.difference: The psalm is sung for the Sabbath, a weekly day of rest, and some hear owning up inside its word for thanks. Muslims weave thanks through five daily prayers, with Friday as the day of gathering.
neighbors.shared: thanks said often becomes a way of seeing.

neighbors.heading: the parent of the virtues
neighbors.text: Today's psalm said it is good to give thanks. The Roman orator Cicero went further: gratitude, he said, is not only the greatest of the virtues but the parent of all the others. Some people, with or without a religion, keep gratitude journals for a similar reason: what you thank for, you start to notice.
neighbors.difference: The psalm thanks God, morning and night, on the Sabbath. Cicero was praising gratitude between people, friends and benefactors, as the root of a good life; it can be practiced without naming God.
neighbors.shared: a thankful day starts with noticing.

neighbors.heading: a hundred thousand tongues
neighbors.text: Today Nishmat said even mouths as full of song as the sea couldn't thank God enough. Guru Nanak reaches for the same size. In Japji, he wishes one tongue could become a hundred thousand, and each of those twenty times more, to repeat God's Name again and again. Elsewhere in Japji he sings that God's praises have no end.
neighbors.difference: Nishmat admits defeat, and the admitting is the thanks. For Guru Nanak, repeating the Name is the path itself: step by step, it carries the soul toward union with God.
neighbors.shared: some thanks are too big for one mouth.
neighbors.sources: Guru Nanak, Japji Sahib, pauris 24 and 32 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: if the mountain were ink
neighbors.text: Today Nishmat stretched every part of the body to the size of the world, then admitted it couldn't thank enough. A Hindu hymn to Shiva does the same. If a black mountain were the ink, the ocean the inkpot, a branch of the heavenly tree the pen, the earth the page, and the goddess of learning wrote forever, she still couldn't reach the end of his glories.
neighbors.difference: Nishmat thanks the one God for kindnesses to a people and its ancestors. The hymn praises Shiva's glories, sung by those who worship him as the highest form of the divine.
neighbors.shared: wonder begins where words run out.
neighbors.sources: Shiva Mahimna Stotra, attributed to Pushpadanta (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: said before the community
neighbors.text: Today the Yom Kippur confession was all we: we have been guilty, we have betrayed. Buddhist monks bring their faults to the community too. On uposatha days, at the new and full moon, monks gather to hear their rule recited. Before it, a monk who has broken a rule admits it to a fellow monk, so the community can stand clean together.
neighbors.difference: The Jewish confession is said to God, in the plural, by everyone, because all Israel is responsible for one another. A monk admits his own offense to a fellow monk; the aim is a pure community and practice, not a pardon from God.
neighbors.shared: it's easier to own a mistake when others stand with you.
neighbors.sources: Vinaya, the Patimokkha and the uposatha observance (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: one to another
neighbors.text: Today the whole congregation confessed together, even for wrongs one person never did. The letter of James asks Christians for something close: "Confess your faults one to another, and pray one for another, that ye may be healed." And the prayer Jesus taught is plural too: "forgive us our debts, as we forgive our debtors."
neighbors.difference: Christians understand forgiveness as coming through Jesus' death and rising. On Yom Kippur, Jews confess to God together, as one body, and turn from what they did; wrongs against a person also need that person's forgiveness.
neighbors.shared: no one carries their mistakes alone.

neighbors.heading: notes to himself
neighbors.text: Today Rebbe Nachman said: speak alone every day, in the language you really think in. The Roman emperor Marcus Aurelius kept a habit like it. His Meditations read like private notes to himself: plain, honest reminders, arguments and encouragement. A journal can do the same work: a place to say everything, in your own words.
neighbors.difference: Hitbodedut is a conversation with God, Master of the world, even if it's one phrase. Marcus spoke to his own mind, reasoning with himself; a journal needs no listener but you.
neighbors.shared: honest words in your own voice can lift a weight.

neighbors.heading: a conversation between friends
neighbors.text: Today Rebbe Nachman taught talking to God alone, daily, in your own words. Catholics know a practice like it as mental prayer. St. Teresa of Avila described it as nothing but a close sharing between friends: taking time, often alone, with the one we know loves us. The Catechism quotes her when it explains this kind of prayer.
neighbors.difference: Teresa's friend is God known in Jesus, and mental prayer often dwells on his life. Rebbe Nachman's hitbodedut pours out the day to the Master of the world, in Yiddish or any tongue.
neighbors.shared: God can hear the words you actually use.
neighbors.sources: St. Teresa of Avila, Life 8.5, quoted in Catechism of the Catholic Church 2709 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: the offering is God
neighbors.text: Today the Torah said: eat, be satisfied, bless. Hindus bring God to the table too. Before a meal, some families chant a verse from the Bhagavad Gita: the offering is Brahman, the food is Brahman, offered by Brahman into the fire of Brahman. Food is often first offered to God at the home shrine, then eaten as prasad, a gift returned.
neighbors.difference: Birkat HaMazon comes after the meal and traces a people's history, from manna to the land to Jerusalem. The Gita verse comes before, and sees the whole act of eating as an offering within Brahman, the one reality.
neighbors.shared: a meal tastes different when it begins or ends in thanks.

neighbors.heading: in the name, and praise after
neighbors.text: Today the Torah's order was eat, be satisfied, then bless. Muslims frame a meal the same way. They begin with bismillah, in the name of God, and end with al-hamdu lillah, praise be to God. Prophet Muhammad taught that God is pleased with a servant who eats a bite and praises Him for it, and drinks a sip and praises Him for it.
neighbors.difference: Birkat HaMazon is a long set blessing in four parts, often sung, and with three at the table one invites the others. The Muslim words are short, said by each person, from the Prophet's own practice.
neighbors.shared: a full plate is a reason to say thank you.

neighbors.heading: first be reconciled
neighbors.text: Today's teaching said teshuvah is specific: one person, one habit, one sentence. Jesus put repair between people before worship itself: "if thou bring thy gift to the altar, and there rememberest that thy brother hath ought against thee; Leave there thy gift before the altar, and go thy way; first be reconciled to thy brother, and then come and offer thy gift."
neighbors.difference: Christians understand forgiveness as flowing from God's mercy in Jesus. In the ten days, Jews return to God through steps like Maimonides', and wrongs against another person need that person's forgiveness too.
neighbors.shared: the gift can wait; the person can't.

neighbors.heading: everyone makes mistakes
neighbors.text: Today's ten days were for turning back, one specific change at a time. Guru Nanak said it plainly: everyone makes mistakes; only the Guru and the Creator don't. Sikhs close the Ardas asking forgiveness for errors made. And a Sikh who breaks a vow can stand before five respected Sikhs, accept a penance, and be welcomed back.
neighbors.difference: Judaism sets aside ten days each year, from the new year to Yom Kippur, for this turning. Sikhs keep no such season; forgiveness is asked daily, and the Guru's grace and the sangat help a person begin again.
neighbors.shared: a mistake is a place to turn, not a place to stay.
neighbors.sources: Guru Nanak, Sri Raag, Guru Granth Sahib Ang 61 (paraphrase) · the Ardas (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: they did penance
neighbors.text: Today Nineveh turned, and God saw their works. Catholics read Nineveh's story too. Jesus pointed to it: the men of Nineveh, he said, did penance at the preaching of Jonah. In Lent, the Church reads Jonah's story beside those words, asking every listener for the same kind of turning: a changed life, not just ashes.
neighbors.difference: For Catholics, Jesus is the one greater than Jonah whom the passage names, and Lent prepares for his death and rising. On Yom Kippur, Jews read Jonah to hear that God's mercy reaches even Israel's enemy.
neighbors.shared: anyone, anywhere, can still turn around.
neighbors.sources: Matthew 12:41 (Douay-Rheims; also Luke 11:32) · Jonah 3 with Luke 11:29–32, read in the first week of Lent (description)

neighbors.heading: even Angulimala
neighbors.text: Today even Nineveh turned, and God saw their deeds change. Buddhists tell of a man everyone feared: Angulimala, a bandit who killed travelers. The Buddha walked straight toward him, unafraid. Angulimala laid down his sword, became a monk, and lived so gently that the text sings of him: one who stops doing harm lights up the world, like the moon freed from a cloud.
neighbors.difference: Nineveh is spared by God's mercy when its people change. Angulimala changes through the Buddha's teaching and his own practice, yet his past deeds still bring him pain; no creator pardons them.
neighbors.shared: no one is too far gone to begin again.

neighbors.heading: Abraham's honored guests
neighbors.text: Today the sukkah welcomed Abraham, who ran from his tent to greet strangers. Muslims honor him as a host too. The Qur'an asks: has the story of Abraham's honored guests reached you? Strangers arrive and say peace; he answers peace, then hurries to his household and brings a fatted calf. The guests turn out to be angels with good news.
neighbors.difference: In the sukkah, Abraham is the guest, a mystical visitor whose portion goes to the poor. In the Qur'an he's the host, a prophet Muslims call the Friend of God, and his guests bring news of a son.
neighbors.shared: keep a seat open for someone you didn't expect.

neighbors.heading: keep a good person in view
neighbors.text: Today the sukkah set a place for heroes of the past. The Roman philosopher Seneca suggested a quieter version. Choose someone good, he wrote to a friend, and keep them always before your eyes: live as if they were watching, act as if they could see. A wise guest at your table, even an imagined one, changes how you behave.
neighbors.difference: The ushpizin are holy ancestors, welcomed in the mystics' telling as real visitors, and their portion goes to real guests in need. Seneca's guest is an exercise of the mind, a model you picture to steady yourself.
neighbors.shared: who you invite in shapes who you become.

neighbors.heading: the lights of freedom
neighbors.text: Today the Hanukkah lamp went in the window, to be seen from the street. Sikhs light up the night too. On Bandi Chhor Divas, they remember Guru Hargobind's release from prison at Gwalior, when, Sikh tradition says, he walked out with fifty-two kings holding on to his cloak. Homes and gurdwaras glow with lamps, and so does the Golden Temple.
neighbors.difference: Hanukkah's lights publicize a miracle: the Temple rededicated and the oil that lasted. Bandi Chhor's lights celebrate freedom shared, because, as the story goes, the Guru wouldn't leave without the other prisoners.
neighbors.shared: good news deserves a light in the window.
neighbors.sources: Sikh tradition of Bandi Chhor Divas (description)

neighbors.heading: lamps at the door
neighbors.text: Today the Hanukkah lights went by the doorway, facing the street. Hindus set lamps at doors and windows too, for Diwali: rows of little clay diyas against the dark. Many tell it as Rama coming home, with the night lit to welcome him. An old Upanishad prayer fits the evening: lead me from darkness to light.
neighbors.difference: Hanukkah remembers a rededicated Temple and a little oil that lasted eight nights. Diwali's stories differ by region and family: Rama's return, Lakshmi's blessing, light winning over darkness.
neighbors.shared: a small flame can say something to a whole street.

items.lessonTitle: Purim: two gifts to the poor

neighbors.heading: if you knew what I know
neighbors.text: Today Maimonides said gifts to the poor outrank your own feast. Buddhists put giving first too: dana, generosity, opens many lists of the path. The Buddha said that if people knew, as he did, the fruit of giving and sharing, they wouldn't eat without sharing, not even their last bite, if someone were there to receive it.
neighbors.difference: On Purim, gifts to the poor are a commandment of one joyful day, at least two gifts to two people. For Buddhists, giving loosens the grip of craving, and its good fruit follows in this life and beyond.
neighbors.shared: joy grows when it's shared with someone in need.

neighbors.heading: call the poor to the feast
neighbors.text: Today the Purim feast came with a rule: give to the poor, and give more than you spend on yourself. Jesus said something close about feasts: "But when thou makest a feast, call the poor, the maimed, the lame, the blind: And thou shalt be blessed; for they cannot recompense thee." A gift to someone who can't pay it back.
neighbors.difference: Jesus invites the poor to the table itself and promises repayment at the resurrection of the just. On Purim, the feast and the gifts are separate mitzvot, and the gifts help the poor hold a feast of their own.
neighbors.shared: the best guest is one who can't pay you back.

items.lessonTitle: Passover: as if you left (Mishnah Pesachim 10:5)

neighbors.heading: stepping into the story
neighbors.text: Today the seder asked each person to see themselves as if they left Egypt. The philosopher Adam Smith described the power behind that. We can't feel another's pain directly, he wrote, so by imagination we place ourselves in their situation and feel something of what they feel. Imagination is where fellow-feeling begins.
neighbors.difference: The seder is a commanded memory of one people's freedom, and it turns into thanks to God. Smith was describing a human gift, sympathy, that reaches toward anyone, with or without faith.
neighbors.shared: a story becomes yours when you step inside it.
neighbors.sources: Adam Smith, The Theory of Moral Sentiments, part 1, section 1, chapter 1 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: present and real
neighbors.text: Today the Mishnah said: in every generation, see yourself as if you came out of Egypt. The Catholic Church points to this very night to explain its own memory. The Catechism says that in the liturgy, the events remembered become in a certain way present and real, and that this is how Israel understands Passover. Catholics say the same of the Mass.
neighbors.difference: For Catholics, the memorial is Christ's Passover, his death and resurrection, made present in the Eucharist. At the seder, Jews remember their own going out of Egypt, by eating, reclining and praising God.
neighbors.shared: remembering can bring the past into the room.

items.lessonTitle: Shavuot: a wedding at the mountain

neighbors.heading: a dream of a wedding
neighbors.text: Today the rabbis pictured Sinai as a wedding, God the groom and the people the bride. Hindus know love poems like that. The Tamil poet-saint Andal sang a dream of her own wedding to Vishnu: the drums, a canopy hung with pearl garlands, her hand taken, the walk around the fire. For her, loving God was a marriage.
neighbors.difference: At Sinai, the bride is a whole people, and the gift is the Torah to live by. Andal's wedding is one devotee's love, and Sri Vaishnava tradition says she was united with the Lord at Srirangam.
neighbors.shared: love is one of the oldest ways to speak of God.
neighbors.sources: Andal, Nachiyar Tirumoli, the "Varanam Ayiram" hymn (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: the mount above them
neighbors.text: Today the Talmud pictured the mountain held over the people at Sinai. The Qur'an tells it too. Speaking to the Children of Israel, it recalls the covenant made with them, the mount raised above them, and the words: hold fast to what We have given you, and remember what is in it. Believers in the Qur'an answer: we hear, and we obey.
neighbors.difference: The rabbis later softened the mountain into a wedding canopy, a covenant of love. Muslims honor the Torah as given to Moses, and see the Qur'an, revealed to Muhammad, as God's final word.
neighbors.shared: a promise is easier to keep when you hold it together.

neighbors.heading: love God, love your brother
neighbors.text: Today the Talmud said the second Temple fell to baseless hatred, even among people who prayed and studied. A letter in the New Testament makes the same sharp point: "If a man say, I love God, and hateth his brother, he is a liar." Prayer and contempt can't share one heart, it says; love starts with the brother you can see.
neighbors.difference: John roots this in God's love: we love because he first loved us, shown in Jesus. The Talmud reads a catastrophe as a warning to its own community, and Tisha B'Av mourns it with a fast.
neighbors.shared: hatred for no reason can be undone by kindness for no reason.

neighbors.heading: no one is my enemy
neighbors.text: Today the Talmud named what tore the second Temple down: hatred with no good reason. Sikhs sing the opposite. Guru Arjan wrote: no one is my enemy, and no one is a stranger; I get along with everyone. The opening line of the Guru Granth Sahib calls God nirvair, without hatred, and Sikhs try to live that way.
neighbors.difference: The Talmud looks back at a catastrophe and asks its own community to change. Guru Arjan speaks of what happens inside one who keeps holy company: seeing one Light in all, enmity falls away.
neighbors.shared: no one is a stranger once you look closely.
neighbors.sources: Guru Arjan, Raag Kanara, Guru Granth Sahib Ang 1299 (paraphrase) · Mool Mantar, Guru Granth Sahib Ang 1

neighbors.heading: let your yes be yes
neighbors.text: Today Israel's leaders kept an oath, even after learning it was won by a trick. Catholics hold a spoken word sacred too. Jesus taught: "But let your speech be yea, yea: no, no." The Church teaches that God's name must never be used to back a lie, and that a promise made before him binds.
neighbors.difference: Joshua's leaders swore by God's name and stood by it. Jesus asked his followers to need no oath at all, just a plain yes; the Church still allows an oath for serious reasons, like in court.
neighbors.shared: a word you give is a word others can lean on.
neighbors.sources: Matthew 5:37 (Douay-Rheims) · Catechism of the Catholic Church 2147, 2150, 2154 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: an empty dipper
neighbors.text: Today a promise held even when keeping it cost something. Buddhists guard their word as training. The Buddha once showed his son Rahula a dipper with a little water in it, then tipped it out: that's how empty the practice becomes of someone who lies on purpose without shame. Not lying is one of the five precepts.
neighbors.difference: Israel's leaders kept the oath because they had sworn by God, and breaking it would shame his name. Buddhism doesn't swear by a God; truthful speech is a precept you take on to train your own mind.
neighbors.shared: the truth you keep keeps you, too.

neighbors.heading: verify it first
neighbors.text: Today the tribes nearly went to war over an altar, until someone went and asked. The Qur'an gives the same counsel: "O ye who believe! If an evil-liver bring you tidings, verify it, lest ye smite some folk in ignorance and afterward repent of what ye did." The next verses call believers to make peace between quarreling brothers.
neighbors.difference: In Joshua, the tribes hear of the altar and gather for war, then send Phinehas and the leaders to ask face to face. The Qur'an makes checking a report a standing rule for believers, before anyone acts.
neighbors.shared: ask before you strike; the story may not be what you think.

neighbors.heading: not the thing, the reading of it
neighbors.text: Today an altar looked like betrayal, and turned out to be a plea: our children belong too. The Stoic Epictetus put the lesson in one line: "Men are disturbed not by the things which happen, but by the opinions about the things." The tribes' fear came from their reading of a pile of stones. One honest conversation changed the reading.
neighbors.difference: In Joshua, peace comes when the eastern tribes answer in God's name and the others say the Lord is among them. Epictetus puts the work in your own judgments: you check your opinion, with or without a God.
neighbors.shared: the story in your head deserves one honest question first.

neighbors.heading: why call her less?
neighbors.text: Today Deborah, a judge, chose to call herself "a mother in Israel." Sikhs honor that word too. Guru Nanak sang that we are born of woman, befriended and married through woman, and that through her the generations go on. Then he asked: why call her lesser, from whom kings are born?
neighbors.difference: Deborah's song honors one woman who rose to lead in a dark time. Guru Nanak's hymn speaks of every woman, against a habit of looking down on women, and says only the True One is beyond being born of one.
neighbors.shared: honor the ones who bring us into the world.
neighbors.sources: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 473, Asa di Var (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: let your mother be a god to you
neighbors.text: Today Deborah chose a word from home and called herself "a mother in Israel." Hindu teaching holds that word high too. In the Taittiriya Upanishad, a teacher sends students home with a few lines to live by, and the first is: let your mother be as a god to you. Then the father, the teacher, and the guest.
neighbors.difference: Deborah's "mother" describes how she leads a whole people: care before command. The Upanishad's line is about how each child honors their own mother, a duty of the home.
neighbors.shared: a mother's care deserves a place of honor.

neighbors.heading: not by birth
neighbors.text: Today Hannah sang of the poor raised out of the dust. Buddhists tell of the Buddha turning birth-rank upside down too. Called an outcast by a proud man, he answered that no one is an outcast by birth, and no one noble by birth: by deeds one becomes an outcast, by deeds a noble one.
neighbors.difference: In Hannah's song, God does the lifting, by his own hand. In the Buddha's teaching, no one lifts you: your own actions make you high or low, and anyone can walk the path.
neighbors.shared: where you start doesn't decide where you belong.

neighbors.heading: the lowly lifted up
neighbors.text: Today Hannah sang that God raises the poor from the dust and seats them with princes. Christians sing a song that echoes hers. When Mary, pregnant with Jesus, visits her cousin Elizabeth, she sings: "He hath put down the mighty from their seats, and exalted them of low degree. He hath filled the hungry with good things."
neighbors.difference: Hannah sings over Samuel, the son she prayed for, and of a king not yet born. Christians hear Mary's song, the Magnificat, as praise for Jesus, whom they believe is the promised king; Jewish tradition doesn't read it that way.
neighbors.shared: nobody is too low to be lifted.

neighbors.heading: what you agree to attend to
neighbors.text: Today a boy learned one sentence: "Speak; for Thy servant heareth." Not a request, just attention. The psychologist William James saw how much rides on that: "My experience is what I agree to attend to." What we listen for shapes who we become. Samuel had to learn to turn toward a voice he first mistook for an old man's.
neighbors.difference: Samuel listens for God, a voice that comes from beyond him and carries a message. James describes how any mind works: attention picks what we notice, whatever we believe lies behind it.
neighbors.shared: listening well is a choice you can practice.
neighbors.sources: William James, The Principles of Psychology, ch. 11 (William James 1890)

neighbors.heading: the ear of your heart
neighbors.text: Today Eli taught a boy to answer, "Speak; for Thy servant heareth." Catholic monks begin with listening too. The Rule of St. Benedict opens with one word, listen, and asks the reader to bend the ear of the heart to a teacher's words. Benedictine monks and nuns have lived by that Rule for centuries.
neighbors.difference: Samuel hears God call his name in the night, directly. Benedict's listening is mostly patient and daily: to scripture, to the abbot, to the community, where Catholics believe God speaks too.
neighbors.shared: the first step in any calling is listening.

neighbors.heading: a handful of rice
neighbors.text: Today a prince loved a shepherd "as his own soul" and gave him his own robe, asking nothing back. Hindus tell of a friendship like that. Sudama, a poor schoolmate of Krishna, came to his palace with only a little flattened rice to give. Krishna ran to meet him, washed his feet, and ate the rice with joy.
neighbors.difference: Jonathan and David are two people, the heir giving to the one who will rise. For devotees, Krishna is God himself, so Sudama's story also shows God treasuring the smallest gift given with love.
neighbors.shared: real friends give without keeping score.

neighbors.heading: love for your brother
neighbors.text: Today Jonathan loved David "as his own soul." Muslims keep a saying of the Prophet Muhammad that sounds close: none of you truly believes until he loves for his brother what he loves for himself. Another hadith counts two people who love each other for God's sake among those God will shade on the Day of Judgment.
neighbors.difference: Jonathan's love is told as one friendship, sealed with a covenant between two men. The hadith makes it a measure of faith for every believer, owed to anyone they call brother or sister.
neighbors.shared: want for a friend what you want for yourself.
neighbors.sources: Sahih al-Bukhari, Book of Faith (paraphrase) · Sahih al-Bukhari, hadith of the seven given shade (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: call the lame to the feast
neighbors.text: Today a king sent for a lame man who expected punishment, and gave him a seat at his table, always. Jesus taught a table like that: "when thou makest a feast, call the poor, the maimed, the lame, the blind: And thou shalt be blessed; for they cannot recompense thee."
neighbors.difference: David seats Mephibosheth out of chesed, the loyal love he owes his friend Jonathan. Jesus asks for a table where the guests have no claim at all, and says God will repay it.
neighbors.shared: a seat at the table can change a whole life.

neighbors.heading: everyone sits on the floor
neighbors.text: Today a lame man, sure he'd be punished, was given a place at the king's table for good. Sikhs keep a table open to everyone. In the langar, the free kitchen at the gurdwara, people of any faith or rank sit side by side and eat the same simple meal. Tradition says Guru Amar Das asked even an emperor to eat there first.
neighbors.difference: David's table honors one man for his father's sake, a king choosing his guest. The langar has no host deciding who's worthy: everyone, even an emperor, sits on the same floor as an equal.
neighbors.shared: a shared meal says: you belong here.
neighbors.sources: Sikh tradition of the langar, Guru Amar Das and Akbar (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: bless, and curse not
neighbors.text: Today a man threw stones and curses at a fleeing king, and David said: let him curse. Catholics hear a call like that in Paul's letter: "Bless them that persecute you: bless, and curse not." And on the cross, Jesus prayed for the men putting him to death: Father, forgive them.
neighbors.difference: David holds back partly because he thinks the Lord may have sent the curse, and on his deathbed he doesn't forget Shimei. Catholics are asked to go past restraint, to wish good on the one who curses.
neighbors.shared: you don't have to answer every stone that's thrown.

neighbors.heading: a gift not taken
neighbors.text: Today David let an insult go by without needing to win. Buddhists tell of a man who came and abused the Buddha to his face. The Buddha asked: if you offer guests food and they don't take it, whose is it? Mine, the man said. Then this abuse, the Buddha said, I don't accept. It stays with you.
neighbors.difference: David lets the curses fall because maybe the Lord sent them, and hopes God will repay him with good. The Buddha simply declines the gift, so anger finds no home in his own mind.
neighbors.shared: an insult only lands if you pick it up.

neighbors.heading: increase me in knowledge
neighbors.text: Today Solomon asked God for a listening heart, not riches. Muslims know Solomon, Sulayman, too. The Qur'an tells of David and Solomon judging a dispute over a field, and says: "And We made Solomon to understand." It also teaches a short prayer anyone can say: "My Lord! Increase me in knowledge."
neighbors.difference: In 1 Kings, Solomon is a king who asks for a listening heart. In the Qur'an, Sulayman is honored as a prophet, and his understanding is a gift named in God's own voice.
neighbors.shared: wisdom starts with asking to understand.

neighbors.heading: wise enough to know
neighbors.text: Today the new king called himself a little child, and asked to be able to hear. Socrates said something close. Told by the oracle that no one was wiser than him, he went questioning people famed for wisdom, and concluded: maybe I'm wiser only in this, that I don't think I know what I don't know.
neighbors.difference: Solomon asks God for wisdom and receives it as a gift. Socrates looked for it by questioning people, and found that admitting what you don't know is where it begins.
neighbors.shared: a humble mind has room to learn.

neighbors.heading: by listening
neighbors.text: Today God wasn't in the wind, the earthquake or the fire, but in "a still small voice." Sikh teaching prizes quiet listening too. In the Japji, Guru Nanak praises listening: by listening, he sings, sorrow and wrongdoing are erased. He names the quiet hours before dawn as the time to meditate on the True Name.
neighbors.difference: Elijah hears a voice that comes to him and asks him a question. Sikh teaching speaks less of a voice than of the Name, God's presence already within, found by quieting the mind's noise.
neighbors.shared: the quiet is sometimes where the voice is.
neighbors.sources: Guru Granth Sahib, Japji Sahib, pauris 4 and 8-11, Ang 2-3 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: hidden in the heart
neighbors.text: Today the noise came three times, and God wasn't in it; then came a voice quiet enough to miss. Hindu teaching listens inward too. The Katha Upanishad says the Self, smaller than small and greater than great, is hidden in the heart of every creature, seen by one who grows free of craving and grief.
neighbors.difference: For Elijah, God speaks from outside him, and he wraps his face in his cloak. In the Upanishad, what's found in the heart is the deepest Self, which some Hindu schools teach is one with Brahman.
neighbors.shared: some truths only come when we're still.

neighbors.heading: the robe and the bowl
neighbors.text: Today a teacher was taken up, and his student picked up the cloak that fell. Buddhists tell a passing-on story too. In the Platform Sutra, the Fifth Patriarch of Chan secretly gives his robe and bowl to Huineng, a poor, unlettered worker from the rice mill, as a sign that the teaching now rests with him.
neighbors.difference: Elisha asks for a double portion of Elijah's spirit, from the God of Elijah. In Chan the robe is only a sign; the teaching passes mind to mind, and the sutra says the robe itself stopped being handed on.
neighbors.shared: what a teacher gives you, you carry forward.
neighbors.sources: Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch, chapter 1 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: commit thou to faithful men
neighbors.text: Today Elisha picked up his teacher's mantle and struck the water, and it parted again. Christians keep a chain like that. The apostle Paul writes to his young student Timothy: "the things that thou hast heard of me among many witnesses, the same commit thou to faithful men, who shall be able to teach others also."
neighbors.difference: Elisha receives Elijah's spirit in one dramatic moment, with a whirlwind and fire. Paul's handing-on is slow and ordinary, person to person, carried along, Christians believe, by the Holy Spirit.
neighbors.shared: every teacher was once somebody's student.

neighbors.heading: perpetual peace
neighbors.text: Today Isaiah said war is learned, so it can be unlearned. The philosopher Immanuel Kant hoped so too. In his essay Perpetual Peace he proposed, among other steps, that standing armies should in time be abolished, and that free nations join in a league bound by law. He laid it out as practical steps, not only a hope.
neighbors.difference: Isaiah's peace comes when the nations go up to learn God's ways from Zion. Kant built his case on reason, law and self-interest, a peace people could reach whatever they believed.
neighbors.shared: peace takes work, like iron beaten at a forge.
neighbors.sources: Immanuel Kant, Perpetual Peace, preliminary article 3 and second definitive article (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: war never again
neighbors.text: Today Isaiah pictured weapons beaten into farm tools. Catholics have carried that hope into the world's halls. In 1965 Pope Paul VI stood before the United Nations and pleaded: no more war, war never again. The Catechism calls everyone to pray and work to be freed from war, and names peace the work of justice.
